parts.name: Passage 1
parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1.

Consecutive and Simultaneous Interpreting

A

When encountering a foreign language barrier, people often turn to professionals to translate or interpret for them. The term ‘translation’ can be used broadly for the process of transferring meaning or expression from one language (the source language) into another (the target language), whether the medium is spoken, written or signed. In certain professional contexts, however, a distinction is drawn between people who work with spoken or signed language (interpreters) and those who work with the written language (translators). While both professions involve transferring information from a source language into a target language, they are still considered distinct, and it is hard to find a person who enjoys both. Some writers on translation, indeed, consider the interpreting task to be more suitable for extroverts and the translating task for introverts.

B

Interpreting is today widely known for its use in international political life. When senior ministers from different cultures and language backgrounds meet, the television coverage invariably shows a pair of interpreters hovering in the background. At major conferences, such as the United Nations General Assembly, the presence of headphones is a clear indication that an important linguistic exercise is going on. In everyday circumstances, interpreters are frequently needed too, especially in cosmopolitan societies formed by new generations of immigrants and foreign workers. Often, the business of law courts, hospitals, local health clinics, classrooms or industrial tribunals cannot be carried on without interpreters. Given the importance and frequency of this work, it is remarkable that so little study has been made of what actually happens when interpreting takes place, and of how successful an exercise it is.

C

There are two categories of interpretation: consecutive and simultaneous. In a consecutive mode of interpreting, the interpreter provides the interpretation after the original speech or some section of it has been finished. During the course of the speech, the interpreter has to focus attention on comprehending and analysing its content. Here the length of each segment to be translated makes a difference to the interpreter's strategies and outcomes. If the segment is just one sentence or two, the interpreter closely follows the original speech. Nevertheless, the interpreter is often expected to translate a long speech which may last for many minutes or even longer. Faced with this situation, he has to remember a great number of messages and keep them in mind until he begins his translation. For this to be possible, the interpreter must record key information using a system of symbols. Studying and practising this set of symbols is an integral part of interpreter training and a special exercise to improve memory.

D

Consecutive interpreting, which is widely employed in informal situations, as well as in committee meetings and small conferences, presumably dates from the Tower of Babel. In this kind of interpretation, the interpreter translates after the speaker has finished speaking. It does break the rhythm of the original language, but that is the nature of it. In larger and more formal events, therefore, where the meaning needs to be delivered effectively and accurately, it has been generally replaced by simultaneous interpreting, whose development arose from the availability of modern audio equipment and the growth of international interaction following the Second World War.

E

The simultaneous mode has attracted great interest because of the complexity of the task and the remarkable skills required. In no other context of human communication is anyone routinely required to listen and speak at the same time, preserving an exact semantic correspondence between the two procedures. Strictly speaking, the term ‘simultaneous’ does not accurately describe the process. Actually, the interpreter might not be able to utter even a single word until the interpreter has grasped enough of the meaning, and he needs time to assimilate what is being said in the source language and to convert it into an acceptable form in the target language, so there is invariably a delay of a few words between the stimulus and the response. This ‘ear-voice span’ is usually about 2 or 3 seconds, but it may be as much as 10 seconds or so if the text is complex. The brain has to memorise what has just been said, attend to what is currently being said, and anticipate the construction of what is about to be said.

F

How it is all done is not at all clear. That it is done at all is a source of some wonder, given the often lengthy periods of interpreting required, the confined environment of the interpreting booth, the presence of background noise, and the awareness that important decisions may depend on the accuracy of the interpretation. Other considerations, such as cultural background, also require interpreters to pay close attention to the backgrounds of speakers and listeners and to differences between the source and target languages.

G

Recent research has now begun to look at how far these factors and the speed at which the source language is spoken affect interpreting performance. It seems that an input speed of between 100 and 120 words per minute is a comfortable rate for interpreting with an upper limit of around 200 w.p.m. Even small changes in speed can dramatically affect the accuracy of output. In one controlled study, when speeds were gradually increased in a series of stages from 95 to 194 w.p.m., the ear-voice span also extended with each stage, and the amount correctly interpreted showed a clear decline. Moreover, as the translating load increased, not only were there more errors of commission, such as mistranslations and vague renderings, there were also more omissions. These are significant findings, considering the need for accuracy and precision in international communication. What is needed is a more detailed identification of the problem areas, and of the strategies speakers, listeners and interpreters adopt to solve them. There is an urgent need to investigate further what has so far been one of the most neglected fields of communication research.

parts.name: Passage 2
parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2.

How Fish Swim

A. The underwater world presents many challenges, one of the most basic being movement. The density of water makes it difficult for animals to move, and forward movement requires a complex interaction of forces. In addition, water itself moves, and strong currents can easily sweep creatures away. These challenges result in a variety of swimming methods used by a wide range of aquatic animals, creating a dazzling underwater ballet.

B. Fish rely on their skeletons, fins and muscles to move. The primary function of the skeleton is to aid the movement of other body parts. The skull acts as a fulcrum, and the vertebrae act as levers. The vertebral column consists of a series of vertebrae held together by ligaments, but not so tightly as to prevent slight sideways movement between each pair of vertebrae. The whole spine is therefore flexible. The skull is the only truly fixed part of a fish. It does not itself move but acts as a point of stability for the other bones. These bones act as levers that enable movement of the fish’s body.

C. While the bones provide the framework for movement, the muscles supply the power. A typical fish has hundreds of muscles running in all directions throughout its body. This is why a fish can turn, twist and change direction quickly. The muscles on either side of the spine contract alternately in sequence from head to tail, causing a wave-like movement to pass down the body. Such movement may be very pronounced in fish such as eels, but hardly perceptible in others, such as mackerel. The frequency of these waves varies from about 50 per minute in the dogfish to 170 per minute in the mackerel. As the head and body thrust sideways and backwards against the water, the water exerts an opposing force that pushes the fish sideways and forwards. When the corresponding set of muscles on the other side contracts, the fish experiences a similar force from the water on that side. The two sideways forces are equal and opposite, unless the fish is turning, so they cancel each other out, leaving the two forward forces to combine.

D. The muscles involved in swimming are of two main types. The bulk of a fish's body is composed of so-called white muscle, while red muscle occurs in much smaller areas at the roots of the fins and in a strip along the centre of each flank. Red muscle receives a good supply of blood and contains larger quantities of fat and glycogen, the latter being a storage form of glucose. Red muscle is used for most day-to-day swimming movements. In contrast, white muscle has a poor blood supply and fewer energy stores, and is used largely for short-term, fast swimming. It might seem odd that an animal so efficiently adapted to its environment should be composed almost entirely of a type of muscle that it rarely uses. However, this huge auxiliary power pack is of crucial importance when the fish is threatened—for example, by a predator—because it enables the fish to swim rapidly away from danger.

E. The fins are among the most distinctive features of a fish. They consist of bony spines protruding from the body and covered by skin, which joins them together either in a webbed form, as in most bony fish, or in a more flipper-like form, as in sharks. Although fins play an important role in swimming, most propulsive movement is produced by the muscular body as a whole, and in only a few fish do the fins contribute significant propulsive force. Their main function is to maintain stability and control direction. As water passes over its body, a fish uses its fins to guide its movement in the direction it wishes to go.

F. Fins located in different parts of a fish serve different purposes, such as moving forwards, turning and maintaining an upright position. The tail fin, in its final lash, may contribute as much as 40 per cent of the forward thrust. The median fins, particularly the dorsal and anal fins, control rolling and yawing movements by increasing the vertical surface area presented to the water. The paired fins—the pectoral and pelvic fins—act as hydroplanes and control the pitch of the fish. Depending on the angle at which they are held relative to the water, they can cause the fish to move downwards or upwards. The pectoral fins lie in front of the centre of gravity and, being readily mobile, are chiefly responsible for directing the fish up or down. The paired fins also enable the fish to slow down and stop.

G. The swimming speed of fish is not always as high as one might expect from watching their rapid movements in aquaria or ponds. Tuna have been recorded at about 44 mph, trout at 23 mph, pike at 20 mph for short bursts and roach at about 10 mph, while the majority of small fish probably do not exceed 2 or 3 mph. Many attempts have been made to measure accurately the speeds at which different fish swim, either by timing them over known distances in their natural environment or by determining their performance in artificial swimming channels. From these studies, fish can be broadly categorised into four groups: “sneakers”, such as eels, which are capable only of slow speeds but have some staying power; “stayers”, which can swim quite fast over long periods; “sprinters”, such as pike, which can generate short bursts of high speed; and “crawlers”, such as bream, which are generally sluggish swimmers although capable of slight acceleration.

H. A species of sailfish is considered to be the fastest fish over short distances, reaching 68 mph over a three-second period, while anglers have recorded speeds above 40 mph over longer periods for several species of tuna. Swimming ability is often considered in relation to body size. Relative to its size, a small fish is generally a more capable swimmer than a much larger one. In terms of absolute speed in miles per hour, however, a large fish will, all other things being equal, be able to swim faster than a smaller fish.

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2.

How Fish Swim

A. The underwater world presents many challenges, one of the most basic being movement. The density of water makes it difficult for animals to move, and forward movement requires a complex interaction of forces. In addition, water itself moves, and strong currents can easily sweep creatures away. These challenges result in a variety of swimming methods used by a wide range of aquatic animals, creating a dazzling underwater ballet.

B. Fish rely on their skeletons, fins and muscles to move. The primary function of the skeleton is to aid the movement of other body parts. The skull acts as a fulcrum, and the vertebrae act as levers. The vertebral column consists of a series of vertebrae held together by ligaments, but not so tightly as to prevent slight sideways movement between each pair of vertebrae. The whole spine is therefore flexible. The skull is the only truly fixed part of a fish. It does not itself move but acts as a point of stability for the other bones. These bones act as levers that enable movement of the fish’s body.

C. While the bones provide the framework for movement, the muscles supply the power. A typical fish has hundreds of muscles running in all directions throughout its body. This is why a fish can turn, twist and change direction quickly. The muscles on either side of the spine contract alternately in sequence from head to tail, causing a wave-like movement to pass down the body. Such movement may be very pronounced in fish such as eels, but hardly perceptible in others, such as mackerel. The frequency of these waves varies from about 50 per minute in the dogfish to 170 per minute in the mackerel. As the head and body thrust sideways and backwards against the water, the water exerts an opposing force that pushes the fish sideways and forwards. When the corresponding set of muscles on the other side contracts, the fish experiences a similar force from the water on that side. The two sideways forces are equal and opposite, unless the fish is turning, so they cancel each other out, leaving the two forward forces to combine.

D. The muscles involved in swimming are of two main types. The bulk of a fish's body is composed of so-called white muscle, while red muscle occurs in much smaller areas at the roots of the fins and in a strip along the centre of each flank. Red muscle receives a good supply of blood and contains larger quantities of fat and glycogen, the latter being a storage form of glucose. Red muscle is used for most day-to-day swimming movements. In contrast, white muscle has a poor blood supply and fewer energy stores, and is used largely for short-term, fast swimming. It might seem odd that an animal so efficiently adapted to its environment should be composed almost entirely of a type of muscle that it rarely uses. However, this huge auxiliary power pack is of crucial importance when the fish is threatened—for example, by a predator—because it enables the fish to swim rapidly away from danger.

E. The fins are among the most distinctive features of a fish. They consist of bony spines protruding from the body and covered by skin, which joins them together either in a webbed form, as in most bony fish, or in a more flipper-like form, as in sharks. Although fins play an important role in swimming, most propulsive movement is produced by the muscular body as a whole, and in only a few fish do the fins contribute significant propulsive force. Their main function is to maintain stability and control direction. As water passes over its body, a fish uses its fins to guide its movement in the direction it wishes to go.

F. Fins located in different parts of a fish serve different purposes, such as moving forwards, turning and maintaining an upright position. The tail fin, in its final lash, may contribute as much as 40 per cent of the forward thrust. The median fins, particularly the dorsal and anal fins, control rolling and yawing movements by increasing the vertical surface area presented to the water. The paired fins—the pectoral and pelvic fins—act as hydroplanes and control the pitch of the fish. Depending on the angle at which they are held relative to the water, they can cause the fish to move downwards or upwards. The pectoral fins lie in front of the centre of gravity and, being readily mobile, are chiefly responsible for directing the fish up or down. The paired fins also enable the fish to slow down and stop.

G. The swimming speed of fish is not always as high as one might expect from watching their rapid movements in aquaria or ponds. Tuna have been recorded at about 44 mph, trout at 23 mph, pike at 20 mph for short bursts and roach at about 10 mph, while the majority of small fish probably do not exceed 2 or 3 mph. Many attempts have been made to measure accurately the speeds at which different fish swim, either by timing them over known distances in their natural environment or by determining their performance in artificial swimming channels. From these studies, fish can be broadly categorised into four groups: “sneakers”, such as eels, which are capable only of slow speeds but have some staying power; “stayers”, which can swim quite fast over long periods; “sprinters”, such as pike, which can generate short bursts of high speed; and “crawlers”, such as bream, which are generally sluggish swimmers although capable of slight acceleration.

H. A species of sailfish is considered to be the fastest fish over short distances, reaching 68 mph over a three-second period, while anglers have recorded speeds above 40 mph over longer periods for several species of tuna. Swimming ability is often considered in relation to body size. Relative to its size, a small fish is generally a more capable swimmer than a much larger one. In terms of absolute speed in miles per hour, however, a large fish will, all other things being equal, be able to swim faster than a smaller fish.

parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3.

The Good-Enough Mother

Throughout history, new parents have experienced the pressures and responsibilities that come with rearing a child. Mothers in particular, for biological and societal reasons, are under pressure to fulfil the expectations that they and society place on them. Donald Winnicott, a British paediatrician and psychoanalyst, broke new ground with his original views on the relationship between children and their mothers, departing from prevailing ideas about parenting. Rather than endorsing the traditional and idealised view of parenting, he offered a theoretical approach and guidance that were more grounded in the realities of parenthood. Winnicott’s notions of the ‘good-enough’ mother and the facilitating environment that he described remain important in the study of child development.

It would not be an exaggeration to say that most parents try to provide the best they can for their children, and many feel guilty when they are unable to do so, especially as many women and men in the modern world try to balance their personal and professional lives with the ideal of perfect parenthood. As a result, parenting has been intensively studied and various theories of parenting have been developed. While a variety of models have informed the development of parenting programmes, four theoretical approaches commonly underpin many of them.

Social learning theory is based on the assumption that children’s behaviour will improve when it is appropriately reinforced: good behaviour is rewarded, while bad behaviour is either ignored or appropriately sanctioned. Programmes based on social learning theory teach parents strategies for managing misconduct and reinforcing positive behaviour.

Attachment theory is based on the notion that an infant’s ability to form a strong emotional bond with their primary caregiver is a natural part of their development. The security of this bond, also known as attachment security, is largely determined by how sensitively and appropriately parents respond to their infant’s bids for attention. Programmes based on attachment theory therefore aim to improve parental sensitivity by increasing parents’ understanding of their children’s needs and attachment-related behaviour.

Parenting styles theory is based on research suggesting that children’s behaviour is directly related to their parents’ child-rearing practices. Parents who combine high levels of parental warmth with high levels of supervision are likely to have children who are more confident, more autonomous and more socially responsible. This parenting style is often referred to as an authoritative style of parenting and recognises the child as an individual in their own right. For this reason, many parenting programmes include elements that encourage parents to allow their children to engage in risk-taking while remaining under close supervision.

The model of human ecology assumes that a child’s development is determined by their interaction with individual, family, school, community and cultural environments. Each of these environments contains elements that can either improve a child’s life outcomes or place them at risk of adversity. Every family has its own combination of risk and protective factors. Programmes based on this model consider ways to strengthen protective factors in order to manage any ongoing risks.

Winnicott’s idea of a facilitating environment created for a child by a ‘good-enough mother’, supported by the adults around her, has clear affinities with attachment theory. For Winnicott, this facilitating environment arises from an unconscious process within an ordinary mother who is fond of her baby. He suggests that during pregnancy, a mother develops a state of heightened sensitivity, which continues for some weeks after the baby’s birth. When this heightened state passes, the mother experiences what Winnicott calls a ‘flight into sanity’ and becomes aware of the world beyond her state of primary maternal preoccupation with her infant.

The good-enough mother continues to provide an environment that supports the baby’s healthy maturational processes. She protects the baby from unpredictable disruptions and provides care through holding, handling and the general management of the child. In addition to meeting the baby’s physical needs, she provides emotional warmth and love. She must also protect the baby from the consequences of the hostile, even murderous, feelings that may arise in her when, for example, the baby screams and cries continuously. By containing these hateful feelings rather than acting on them, she can use her awareness of them to understand the baby’s own terror and hate. At first, she adapts closely to the baby’s needs, allowing the baby to experience a sense of omnipotence. As the baby gradually begins to feel secure enough to relinquish this sense of omnipotence, the process of integration can begin, and the baby starts to develop a distinction between ‘me’ and ‘not me’. To support this development, the good-enough mother must gradually ‘fail’ to adapt fully to the baby’s needs, allowing the baby to learn to tolerate the frustrations of the world beyond the mother–infant relationship.

Winnicott intended to take the pressure off mothers, but critics have argued that his idea of the good-enough mother has placed undue expectations on actual mothers, suggesting that they must shoulder most of the responsibility for caring for their babies. Furthermore, mothers are held responsible for how well their babies flourish.

As with many theories of child development, real-life parenting does not fit neatly within a single theoretical model. Most parents display elements associated with several approaches as they adapt naturally to different situations. Nevertheless, Winnicott’s ideas have been a source of comfort and hope to many mothers who have struggled with the challenges of motherhood.
